stem: A 22-year-old woman has recurrent episodic wheezing and nocturnal breathlessness relieved by salbutamol. She is asymptomatic between episodes. Spirometry is performed before and after bronchodilator. Which finding most strongly supports asthma rather than COPD?

keywordsHtml:
1. Episodic wheezing + nocturnal breathlessness → classic pattern of variable airway obstruction suggesting asthma.
  2. Relief with salbutamol → indicates reversibility of bronchoconstriction (key asthma feature).
  3. Spirometry before and after bronchodilator → diagnostic test to assess reversibility (asthma vs COPD differentiation).

D.title: FEV₁ increase ≥12% and ≥200 mL after bronchodilator
D.body:
Asthma is characterized by reversible airflow obstruction due to bronchial hyperresponsiveness and inflammation. The hallmark diagnostic feature is significant bronchodilator reversibility on spirometry, defined as:
Increase in FEV₁ ≥12% AND ≥200 mL from baseline
This confirms reversible airway obstruction, strongly supporting asthma rather than COPD, which typically shows fixed or minimally reversible obstruction.
This is the Gold Standard spirometric criterion for asthma diagnosis. It reflects improved airway caliber after bronchodilator use, confirming reversible bronchospasm. This is the most specific discriminator between asthma and COPD in clinical practice. It directly demonstrates functional reversibility of airway obstruction.

This is the most specific discriminator between asthma and COPD in clinical practice. It directly demonstrates functional reversibility of airway obstruction.

A.title: No significant bronchodilator reversibility
A.body: This finding suggests fixed airflow obstruction, which is more typical of COPD. In asthma, reversibility is expected; thus this option argues against asthma. It represents poor bronchodilator response and does not support asthma diagnosis.
A.bodyHtml: This finding suggests fixed airflow obstruction, which is more typical of COPD. In asthma, reversibility is expected; thus this option argues against asthma. It represents poor bronchodilator response and does not support asthma diagnosis.

B.title: Normal spirometry between attacks
B.body: Asthma patients often have completely normal lung function between episodes, especially in mild disease. However, this is not diagnostic on its own, as COPD may also show near-normal spirometry in early stages. Therefore, it is supportive but not the strongest discriminator.

C.title: Progressive FEV₁ decline over time
C.body: This is characteristic of COPD, reflecting irreversible structural lung damage and progressive airflow limitation. Asthma does not typically show steady decline unless poorly controlled over long periods. This option strongly favors COPD rather than asthma.
C.bodyHtml: This is characteristic of COPD, reflecting irreversible structural lung damage and progressive airflow limitation. Asthma does not typically show steady decline unless poorly controlled over long periods. This option strongly favors COPD rather than asthma.

E.title: Low FEV₁ with reduced DLCO
E.body: Reduced DLCO indicates alveolar destruction (emphysema) or interstitial pathology. Asthma usually has normal or increased DLCO because alveolar-capillary units remain intact. This option strongly supports COPD (especially emphysema), not asthma.

keyConcept: Asthma is diagnosed by reversible airflow obstruction on spirometry, demonstrated by significant improvement in FEV₁ after bronchodilator. COPD, in contrast, shows fixed or minimally reversible obstruction with progressive decline and often reduced DLCO in emphysema.
